query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a single-step equal-channel angular pressing (ECAP) process to the eutectic high-entropy alloy will refine its hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure, reduce dislocation pile-up at semi-coherent phase boundaries, and thereby overcome the intrinsic tensile brittleness while retaining or increasing strength.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a hierarchical microstructure comprising dual-phase lamellar colonies featuring semi-coherent phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: A single-step severe plastic deformation process via equal-channel angular pressing (ECAP).
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under quasi-static loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined dual-phase lamellar architecture with a more homogeneous dislocation distribution and diminished local stress concentrations at internal phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The ECAP process introduces intense shear deformation that refines and reorients the lamellar colonies, breaking up continuous dislocation barriers and mitigating pile-ups at phase boundaries. This leads to a more uniform dislocation density and activates dynamic recovery or reconfiguration in the microstructure. The decreased local stress concentrations reduce premature microcrack initiation, enabling enhanced ductility without sacrificing the strengthening effects imparted by the semi-coherent interfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to exhibit increased yield and ultimate tensile strengths compared to the untreated material along with improved room-temperature tensile ductility, due to alleviated stress concentrations from dislocation pile-ups. The improvement in ductility may be moderate but is targeted to alleviate brittleness under quasi-static loading.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA, characterized by its dual-phase lamellar colonies, shows high strength but limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle failure, primarily due to pronounced dislocation accumulation at internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to conditions of room-temperature, quasi-static tensile deformation; its validity under high strain rates or elevated temperatures remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: While the ECAP process can refine the microstructure, in some conventional alloys it has been observed to reduce ductility; therefore, the net balance between strength and improved ductility in this specific eutectic HEA is uncertain and may depend on optimized processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Process a set of eutectic HEA samples using the ECAP procedure under controlled parameters (e.g., single pass at room temperature with a fixed channel angle) and compare their tensile properties against untreated controls. Conduct detailed microstructural analyses (using SEM/TEM) to assess dislocation distribution and boundary integrity. Perform tensile tests to record stress-strain responses.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, uniform elongation)
Electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) for dislocation structures and phase boundary morphology
Fractographic analysis to identify crack initiation and propagation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ECAP-treated samples do not show a reduction in stress concentrations (i.e., dislocation pile-up) at phase boundaries, or if their tensile ductility is not improved (or is degraded) relative to untreated samples, then the hypothesis will be considered refuted.

In Fig. 1a, a typical tensile engineering stress-strain curve of an as-annealed CG Ni is shown as Curve A. Its mean yield strength is only 53 MPa, but the pronounced strain hardening capability due to dislocation accumulation delays necking to an elongation of the order of 40%. Typical electrodeposited (ED) Ni (Curve B and Curve C) has a higher strength but the uniform elongation decreases with decreasing grain diameter, dgrain. cited_evidence.kind: web:The role of phase boundary in second phase strengthening
cited_evidence.text: It is a traditional method to strengthen alloys by introducing internal boundaries in order to impede the motion of dislocations. Unlike coherent twin boundaries with low excess energies, grain boundaries and phase boundaries are regarded as major strengthening agents for metallic materials because they are more effective in resisting dislocation penetration. In this study, the phase boundaries were produced through the eutectic reaction during the preparation of dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA. Thereby plenty of phase boundaries contained in this HEA were semi-coherent due to the low energy features. Given that interfacial strength increases with the decrease of coherency, phase boundaries of semi-coherence prepared in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were observed to be strong enough to accommodate high stress due to their chemically disordered features, as proved by the HAADF-STEM observation (Fig. 3b) and in-situ straining experiments. Such strong phase boundaries were essential to achieving compatibility of interphase deformations through enhancing the strength of FCC phases by work hardening effects so as to commence dislocation glide in BCC phases.
